activities.caption: pair each quantity with what it physically measures
activities.name: dcQuantityMatch

config.prompt: Three quantities, three physical meanings — pair them:

pairs.right: energy per unit charge — joules per coulomb
the flow of charge itself — coulombs per second
the friction between them — push needed to sustain a given flow
pressure across a pipe run, litres per second, pipe narrowness

config.why: Hold the analogy loosely — electrons do not pour out of wires and drain away, charge cannot spill or splash, and the analogy says nothing about fields. Climb the ladder, then leave it behind.

activities.anchor: Ohm converts local voltage to local current
activities.caption: three V–I lines — which one is the 200 Ω part?
activities.name: dcOhmTrace

config.prompt: V–I lines for three resistors (voltage up, current across). Which line is the 200 Ω resistor?
config.why: Resistance is the slope: at 60 mA the 200 Ω line asks 12 V, the 100 Ω asks 6 V, the 50 Ω asks 3 V — "double the push, double the flow" reads straight off the graph.

activities.anchor: It is not. It is a material
activities.caption: file the components: does Ohm's law hold?
activities.name: dcOhmBuckets

config.prompt: V = IR is a property, not a conservation law. File each case:

items.label: a metal wire at constant temperature
a lightbulb filament as it heats
a metal at a steady cool operating temperature

config.why: A diode ignores the law outright and a heating filament drifts out of line — yet Kirchhoff's laws keep working in circuits where Ohm's law fails everywhere. KCL and KVL are the two pillars; Ohm is the convenient helper.

activities.anchor: Small enough to check by hand
activities.caption: replay the three-law solve in sequence
activities.name: dcSolveOrder

config.prompt: 12 V into a 100 Ω series resistor and two 200 Ω in parallel — put the solve in order:
items: Collapse the parallel pair: 200 ÷ 2 = 100 Ω, so the total is 200 Ω
Ohm's law gives the battery current: 12 ÷ 200 = 60 mA
KVL splits the volts: 0.06 × 100 = 6 V, leaving 6 V across the pair
KCL finishes: 6 V across each 200 Ω branch drives 30 mA per branch
Check: 30 + 30 = 60 mA — balanced at every node
config.why: Ohm converts push into flow, KVL constrains voltages, KCL constrains currents — the same pattern you will later automate with nodal analysis.

activities.caption: one line of the derivation is wrong — find it
activities.name: dcDividerSpot

config.prompt: A pupil derives the divider formula. One line is wrong — click it:
lines: One current flows through both resistors: I = Vin ÷ (R1 + R2)
The output is taken across R2, so Vout = I × R2
Check with the defaults — 9 V, R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 2 kΩ: Vout = 3 V
config.correction: Vout = 9 × 2 ÷ (1 + 2) = 6 V — the tap takes the fraction 2 ÷ 3 of the input.
config.why: The current readout changes with the sum of the resistors, but the output fraction depends on R2 ÷ (R1 + R2) — double R2 and the fraction rises; double R1 and it falls.

activities.caption: fill the power ledger — milliwatts in, milliwatts out
activities.name: dcPowerCloze

config.text: 9 V across 3 kΩ drives %%0%% mA, so the battery delivers %%1%% mW. The 1 kΩ resistor, dropping 3 V, dissipates %%2%% mW; the 2 kΩ, dropping 6 V, takes the other %%3%% mW — and the books balance because KVL is %%4%% wearing a circuit's clothes.
config.hint: P = VI = I²R = V²/R — pick the form that matches the question.

activities.caption: bet the meter reading before the sag is computed
activities.name: dcLoadPredict

config.q: The unloaded tap reads 6 V. Close the load onto it — what does the meter read now?
config.why: 6 × 1000 ÷ 1667 ≈ 3.6 V — a 40 percent sag the naive divider formula never predicted. The cure: divider resistances small compared with the load, shrinking the Thevenin resistance.

config.prompt: A load extracts the most power from a Thevenin source when its resistance equals the Thevenin resistance. What share of the generated power reaches the load at that match point?
config.why: Half — which is fine for a radio antenna and deliberately avoided in a power grid, where matching the generator would waste half the plant.
config.context: Maximum power and maximum voltage transfer are different goals: deliver energy and you avoid the match; deliver information and you design for it.
